strengths: The per-orientation heatmaps reveal informative structure in generalization that aggregate accuracy obscures. The observed roles of nearby views, in-plane rotations, and object symmetry have a clear audience among researchers studying visual robustness and learned representations.

The experimental coverage is substantial: three object families, multiple training-orientation ranges, varying proportions of fully-seen instances, five repetitions, and several architectures. The fixed training-image budget and supplementary pretraining, augmentation, and data-volume controls strengthen the descriptive findings. Cross-category experiments add useful evidence about the breadth of the phenomenon.

The geometric model provides an interpretable account of the observed accuracy patterns, supported by component ablations and high reported correlations. The learning paradigm and principal visualizations communicate the central empirical result clearly, and links to code and data support reuse.
weaknesses: Necessary: Calibrate the mechanistic conclusions. Although the abstract presents dissemination as a hypothesis, Sections 3.3–4 make stronger statements that generalization is driven by transferred invariance through shared features and that biological recognition mechanisms largely apply to DNNs. Correlations between fully-seen invariance, partially-seen invariance, and accuracy are consistent with this explanation, but do not establish the direction of transfer or the functional role of particular features. Shared image geometry and jointly learned representations remain alternative explanations. Retaining the stronger claims requires discriminating evidence, such as targeted feature interventions; otherwise, the conclusions should consistently remain observational and hypothesis-level.

Necessary: Validate the interpretation of the neural invariance metric. Equations 5–7 compare responses averaged over orientation sets. Equal averages can conceal substantial orientation-dependent activity, so a high score does not itself demonstrate an invariant feature detector. Additionally, requiring both averages to exceed the 95th-percentile threshold excludes units that respond strongly in one set but weakly in the other—precisely a potentially important form of non-invariance. Reporting the retained fraction L and checking orientation-level responses and threshold sensitivity would help establish what the metric measures.

Necessary: Distinguish descriptive fitting from predictive validation. Section 2.4 optimizes the model parameters against Pearson correlation with measured network accuracy, and Figures 4 and S5 report that correlation without describing a separate evaluation split. These results demonstrate goodness of fit, but do not establish prediction on unseen experiments or orientations. Specify the fitting and evaluation protocol and either provide held-out validation or narrow the predictive claims. The DNN's own train/test separation does not resolve this separate model-evaluation issue.

Necessary: Resolve the definition of generalizable orientations. Section 2.5 thresholds f_w at 10% of its maximum, although f_w is an uncalibrated sum of logistic functions fitted using an objective insensitive to additive offsets. Consequently, its numerical threshold need not correspond to accuracy above chance. Figure S9c displays scores roughly between 1.8 and 2.4, which also appear incompatible with a nontrivial split at 10% of the maximum unless an additional normalization is applied. Specify that normalization and demonstrate partition stability, because this partition underlies Figure 5. Accuracy separation in Figure S8 is not independent validation when the partition derives from an accuracy-fitted model.

Necessary: Narrow unsupported scope statements. The half-data comparison in Section 2.1 demonstrates stability over the tested data sizes, not that additional data cannot improve performance. Likewise, conclusions about neural networks generally should acknowledge the controlled rendering setup and limited transformer coverage. The descriptive study can be valuable within these boundaries without requiring broader experiments.

Optional: Enlarge the dense labels in Figures 4 and S5–S8 and report numerical correlations with uncertainty, including results within architecture and orientation groups. These changes would make the strength and consistency of the reported relationships easier to assess.
